item.title: Halley's Comet Over New Zealand In 1910: An Overview Of A Spectacular Apparition
item.description: arXiv:2611.33170v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Halley's Comet (1P/Halley) returns to the inner Solar System approximately every 76 years. In 1910, the comet put on a particularly wonderful display, whereby the comet attained an apparent magnitude of 1 or brighter, and had a tail of up to 120{\deg} in length. Many New Zealanders saw Comet 1P/Halley and submitted articles to newspapers across the land. Those articles were mostly from lay-people who reported their observations of this, the most famous of all comets. There were, however, numerous serious amateur and professional astronomers who made detailed observations and took world-class photographs of the comet. In this paper, we present the results of a thorough search through historical records and media publications in Aotearoa/New Zealand, to investigate how extensively Comet 1P/Halley was observed from this island nation. Where appropriate, we compare the observations described with international accounts, and find that those made from Aotearoa/New Zealand often echo what observers were witnessing around the world. We find that thousands of New Zealanders observed Comet 1P/Halley in 1910, and that the comet raised the interest in astronomy across the land resulting in the establishment of a number of astronomical societies that remain active to the current day.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage, 29(3), 563-636 (2026)
item.dc:creator: John Drummond, Wayne Orchiston, Carolyn Brown, Jonathan Horner

item.title: Time Travel Paradoxes and Entangled Timelines
item.description: arXiv:2303.07635v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: For time travel to be consistent with the known laws of physics, the resulting paradoxes must be resolved. It has been suggested that the notion of parallel timelines may provide a resolution, by allowing different events to happen in different timelines. However, so far, a concrete mechanism by which parallel timelines can be created has never been satisfactorily formulated in a way that makes the relationships between the timelines clear. In this paper, we propose such a mechanism based on the Everett (many-worlds) interpretation of quantum mechanics. The timelines in our model are variants of the "worlds" of the Everett interpretation that can connect to each other via the time machine. They are created by the entanglement of the time machine with the environment and the resulting decoherence; therefore, we call them "entangled timelines" or E-CTCs. As the entanglement gradually spreads out to additional systems, the timelines spread out as well, providing a local and well-defined mechanism for branching timelines. The E-CTC model is similar to Deutsch's familiar D-CTC model but differs from it mainly by imposing a different consistency condition, based on pure states, which allows the information about the entanglement to be preserved. These differences allow us to create a clearer practical definition of the timelines and avoid some of the surprising consequences of the D-CTC model's non-linear evolution.
item.dc:creator: Barak Shoshany, Zipora Stober
